title: The Warm Cage
passages:
Teodoro read it out loud, all of it, because that was how he read anything, and nobody at Anza asked him a question they didn't want the whole shop to hear.

"Hold order," he said. "Remand of the live lid-hand, Bay Four, to the coast roster. Collecting vehicle already logged." He tilted the plate so the cathode light bleeding under the back-room door ran across the glass. "Filed at the Kettering morning desk, 05:40."

The plate was the node's list of its own people — name, badge, status — and under each one a strip of small gray type that a desk four hundred kilometers off could write to without asking anybody's leave. Reader two sat below it, the block that read a body's hands and voice and put a name where there hadn't been one. It had put Wren's there an hour ago. She sat against the compressor housing with her wrists still bound in seal tape, saying *thirty-six point four* under her breath, the way a pump says its own pressure.

"There's a second part," Teodoro said.

"Of course there is." Rhea had a respirator cartridge in one fist and grease to the elbow and no intention of putting either down.

"File 2244. Physical recovery. Badge 2244." He read it twice, which he only did when a line surprised him. "It's moving. Deadline pinned to the shift bell."

Behind him the compressor held its note. Ivo was on the other side of that note, on mains power, breathing through a disc of heavy glove rubber cut out of a palm — except the palm belonged to the woman on the floor and the man it was cut around was alive in the next room.

"Chain condition," Teodoro said, and stopped.

"Teodoro."

"Green holds while the remand is executed." He looked up. "It's the food line, Rhea. She rolls at the bell, Anza eats. She doesn't, and the chain drops red at the bell with Brill's canisters still sitting on the truck at the ore stub."

"Eleven seals short," Nour said from the board ledge, not moving, "and now we're short a person."

Coombs stood in the shop doorway with the cold coming in around his boots and said nothing at all, which Rhea distrusted more than talk. Out in the yard his tender rang the quarter. It had a warm sound, that bell, like a kitchen.

"There's a signature field," Teodoro said. "It wants a countersigning badge."

"Fine. Whose?"

"It's already filled in." He turned the plate around so she could see it.

*2244.*

Through the back-room door came the scrape of a boot on plank, and Marlowe's voice, thick with the sedative still coming off him. "Is that the desk? Tell them I'm not signing myself off."

"Nobody's asking you to," Rhea said, to the door, and then, lower, to the plate: "It's not asking him to sign. It's asking us to sign *her*, and it's holding his number over the field like a hand over a stove."

Wren had stopped counting. In the quiet she looked at the glass, at the four digits sitting there, and Rhea watched her understand it a half second before anyone said it out loud — that the desk had made it one trade with two names on it, and that the bell was going to take one of them either way.

"Two days," Teodoro said, because he told you everything he knew. "Recovery's window is two days from the filing. But the deadline's the bell."

The cursor went on blinking under Marlowe's badge. Out in the yard the tender's bell rang again, closer to warm than before, and the plate waited for somebody standing in that room to put a name under it.

Coombs came two steps in out of the weather and stopped there, gloves still on. A man who meant to handle something took his gloves off first, Rhea thought, and filed it where she filed things.

"Lid-hand," he said. He said it the way a man reads a docket out to somebody who can't see the page. "You know what a remand is?"

"It's in the book," Wren said. "You read it out. Everybody heard."

"Then you know it isn't a sentence. It's a bunk." He crouched, which put him level with her without putting him over her, and Rhea gave him that much craft. "Shelf over the motor box. Coolant loop runs right through it, so it's the warmest twelve inches on the Interior. Three meals at whatever node we're tied at, and a coat out of coast stores, because the one you're wearing wouldn't stop a rumor."

"I've been warm."

"Have you."

"In the tool void. It was warm the whole way. Nobody came."

Something moved behind his face and he put it away. He tipped the proving slate out of his coat, the reader that had sung two names off no roster an hour ago, and turned the field toward her.

"The proof," he said. "One to a body. Yours is a walk, a voice, and a count in a bay. I sign the remand, the slate overwrites that with a roster line, and the proof is gone. Not sealed. Not filed down-line where a desk can pull it. Gone." He tilted it a few degrees. "So nobody proves what happened at Bay Four. Not Kettering, not Pell, not the officer with the hat. Not me."

"And not me," Wren said.

"That's the mercy in it."

"That's the part I heard."

"Overwriting's honest," Teodoro said from the plate, because if he knew a thing he said it. "The slate won't carry two claims on one body. It takes the newest and drops the old one clean."

"Your count's on eleven of my short lines," Nour said from the ledge, not looking up. "Four runs. A tally card that comes up short closes with a voice line, because a reader will take a voice where it can't get a seal. There was always a voice."

Wren worked her wrists inside the seal tape, once, the way you test a chain you already know the length of.

"You hold the lid down with both hands," she said, "and you say the number out loud. That's the job. Voss stamped. I said the number." She looked at the slate and not at him. "That's the whole distance between us. It isn't much of one. It's the only one I've got."

"The stamp's in a chair at Kettering with a line-trust officer buying him coffee."

"Then take me on the book's line," Wren said. "Don't sell me the bunk."

"I'm selling you a winter."

"You're selling me a winter I don't have to remember. That's not the same thing and I'm not buying it." She let her head rest back against the compressor housing. "I'm the hands. Not the stamp. Put that in your field and see whether it holds."

"The field wants a badge," Rhea said. "It'll take *hands* if you spell it with a number after."

Coombs stood up, unhurried, a man who had never once had to chase anybody down. That was the thing about him, Rhea thought. He didn't argue. He waited, and the cold did his arguing, and the bell.

"You'll want it by the coast line," he said. "Long dark to the Weir, and you'll be nobody the whole way, and nobody doesn't get fed twice."

"Coombs," Teodoro said.

"I'm being kind."

"You're being *early*," Teodoro said. "The signature field's still open."

Coombs set the slate down on the crate between them, face up, and the lamplight ran across the glass. Two lines on it. Two blanks, side by side, waiting for names.

"Nineteen years I've pulled," he said. "Never once with one."

Behind Wren the number went on under everything, soft and even, the way the compressor did.

Boots on plank, and Miko came in off the ore stub with the cold still standing in the seams of her jacket and her hands up her sleeves. She stopped at the edge of the lamplight, looked at the slate on the crate with its two blanks, then at the woman taped to the compressor.

"Two lines," she said. "Which one's mine, or am I the entertainment?"

"Reyes," Coombs said.

"Tonight I am." She dug in her inside pocket and came out with the tickets, three of them, soft at the folds from being handled, and fanned them across her knuckles like a hand she had no intention of playing. "Dalia Reyes. Ines Salter. Corin Mabry. Three berths on the coast line, paid in full, out of a loader's wage, which ought to tell you something about my judgment." The fan shut. "So here's the arithmetic, since you're a man who likes a book. A green board means the trains are running. It does not mean anybody's hiring. I get to the coast on a name that's good for one berth and no roster line — a roster line being the thing that says a node owes you a bunk and a cookhouse is going to feed you — and I stand on a platform in the dark with a paid seat and nothing in me since Kettering, and the train goes off without me because I'm behind a crate making myself hard to see."

"There's a shelf over the motor box," Coombs said. "Warm side of the coolant loop. You've stood in the doorway and looked at it."

"I've looked at it."

"Then you know I'm not lying about the warm."

"You're not lying about the warm. That's the whole trick of you." Rhea watched her line up something clever, hold it, and set it down unused. "Say I take the bunk. Who pays my wage?"

"The node that logs you."

"Out of what?"

"Out of its own line. You draw against the roster, you work the roster, it comes back to you in work."

Miko turned her head to the board ledge, to Nour, to the tally card lying face-out with its eleven short strokes.

"Nour. What's a line worth this winter?"

"A hundred and ten ration-days," Nour said, without looking up.

"A hundred and ten." Miko said it again slower, the way you check a sum you already know is going to come out bad. "So the warmest twelve inches on the Interior costs this node a hundred and ten meals out of a winter it's already eleven seals short on, and I'd be eating some of them, and Ivo is on the other side of that wall breathing through a piece of a glove." She pushed the tickets back into her coat. "Coombs. First honest thing I've said since Kettering. I can't afford your mercy. It's priced in somebody else's food."

"It's priced in a winter," he said. "You'd have earned it by spring."

"By spring I'd have earned a coat I needed in order to work the winter. That's not a wage, that's a rope with knots in it." She tipped her chin at the slate. "And that thing eats the names with me. Salter, Mabry, gone. Nobody at the coast can pull them."

"Good," Miko said. "Two of them owe money."

Teodoro, who had been quiet for eleven seconds, which for him was a record, said, "Overwriting's clean. There's no pulling it back. Not by me, not by the desk, not by the officer with the hat."

"So you're asking me to be nobody on purpose, and to be warm while I'm at it." Miko rubbed her knuckles where the tickets had sat. "I've been nobody by accident for two days. It's overrated. Nobody doesn't get fed twice."

"Nobody doesn't get caught, either."

"There's that." She looked at the blank with her name on it for a while, and the compressor held its note under everything, and out in the yard the tender's bell rang the half, patient as a stove. "One more question, and it's a real one, so don't waste it. If I go as far as the Weir on your book and then I walk off it — what does that cost you?"

Coombs set the slate down.

"My slate. My name on the file, and a false line under it that I signed." He said it the way a man reads out a docket. "Nobody walks at the Weir. The coast lights are right there across the cut, and the dark's on the other side of them."

"That's the first thing you've said tonight that came out of a book instead of out of you."

She waited for the answer to that. Rhea watched Coombs take off his right glove, finger by finger, without once looking down at his own hand.

The ore stub didn't have a proper office, just a lean-to bolted to the relay wall with a desk that had seen three operators and a radio that picked up Kettering on clear nights and nothing on the others. Kass had been sleeping under it in twenty-minute shifts since the board went red, which meant they knew the smell of the tender before the ramp came down — cold hydraulic fluid, old brake dust, and something underneath it that smelled like the Blank after a rig has sat in it too long.

Doan was already at the belly hatch when they got there, wrist still looped through the locker cord like a dog on a lead. Their clearance had been pulled at 04:00, same as half the node, and the overlap key on their belt was dead weight — withdrawn with the rest of it. They didn't ask why Kass wanted the tender opened. They just braced a shoulder against the cold metal, fingers finding the manual release lip, and hauled until the hatch groaned up on its pistons and locked.

Inside, the tender was clean. Too clean. No cargo straps, no dunnage, no grease pencil marks on the bulkheads. The deck plates lifted on concealed hinges — Kass had to wedge their fingers into the seam and pull, and when they came up there was nothing under them but painted steel and a mount that had never held a transponder.

"Blank mount," Kass said. "Factory cut, not field."

Doan crouched beside them, breath steaming. Their face was doing that thing where it looked calm and their eyes were moving too fast. "Harness?"

"Cut. Clean through the loom, same as the four at Kettering." Kass ran their fingers over the severed ends, counting. "Power, data, beacon, handshake. All four. Whoever built this didn't want it talking to a master board. Didn't want it talking to anything."

"Four rigs," Doan said. "Vanished off the master at 04:51. No alarm. No scrub line."

"Badge 2241 locked on channel the whole time." Kass sat back on their heels. The gravel was cold through their coveralls. "This makes five. A fleet that doesn't post. That doesn't *exist* until somebody with a slate or a key decides it does."

"Coombs's tender."

"Coombs's *tender*." They said it flat. "Nineteen years pulling runners. You don't run a ghost rig that long without a node somewhere signing for it. Which means somebody at a desk has been signing false lines for nineteen years, or the desk itself has a hole in it."

Doan's hand went to their belt, to the dead overlap key. "The morning desk at Kettering. Ospina's authority is flagged there. File 2244 is moving from there."

"Fenn filed compressor priority from Culvert Nine's reader." Kass stood up, wiping their fingers on their thigh. "Voss admitted eleven reseals. Said the taped-glove counter wasn't him. The desk has the stamp, the forger, and the file. What it doesn't have is the fleet."

A light moved at the far end of the stub — the relay shop door opening, spilling cathode glow onto the ore dust. Coombs's silhouette, broad and patient. Behind them, the tender's bell rang the half.

"Five rigs," Doan said quietly. "That we know of. How many more are running the ore line right now, posting to no board, carrying whatever the hell they're carrying?"

Kass looked at the cut harness, at the blank mount, at the clean painted steel that had never held a transponder in its life. They thought of the four rigs that had deleted themselves from Kettering's master board, one by one, like names being erased from a roster. They thought of the glove in their coat pocket, the tape across the knuckle, the clean disc cut from the palm.

"Find out," they said. "That's what I do."

They keyed their radio. "Teodoro. You reading?"

"Always," his voice came back, tinny and tired. "Plate's still open. Bell's at the half."

"Your coast puller's tender is a ghost. No transponder. Blank mount, cut harness — same as the four that vanished off Kettering. There's a fleet of these things, Teo. Living off every book."

A pause. The compressor note held steady through the radio. "Fenn has Voss at Kettering bay three. The officer with the hat."

"Then ask the officer with the hat how many ghost rigs they've signed for. Because if Coombs has been pulling runners for nineteen years on a rig that doesn't exist, the desk didn't just miss it. The desk *made* it."

They clicked off before Teodoro could answer. Doan was watching them, the locker cord tight around their wrist.

"You're not going to drop it," Doan said.

"Never have."

"Even if it puts people at risk."

"Especially then." Kass started for the shop door, the cathode light bleeding across the gravel. "The risk is already here. The question is who signed for it."

Behind them, the tender's bell rang again. Three-quarters. The shop door framed Coombs in the warm light, one glove off, one glove on, waiting like a stove for somebody to put a name in the fire.
